amendments.rule: A substantival article before a participle splits; it does not absorb the clause. `οἱ κατοικοῦντες` → *they that dwell* is `οἱ` → *they* and `κατοικοῦντες` → *that dwell* headed on *dwell*, never one unit taking *they that*. The article supplies the pronoun and nothing else, because the participle is what the relative clause is predicated of. Where **another source token has already written that pronoun** — an expressed pronoun or noun standing in apposition to the article's phrase — nothing is left for the article to supply and it is its own `unrepresented` unit, the participle keeping the supplied relativizer along with any copula and its own verb: `τοῖς δὲ σῳζομένοις ἡμῖν` → *unto us who are saved* gives *unto us* to `ἡμῖν` under rule 21, nothing to the article, and *who are saved* to the participle headed on *saved*. That is rule 20's stated contrast holding where a participle rather than a noun follows the article, `Ὑμῖν … τοῖς ἔθνεσιν` → *to you that are Gentiles* leaving it empty because `ὑμῖν` has written the *you*, and it is the same reading an articular **adjective** in that apposition takes under rules 20 and 92, `αὐτοῖς δὲ τοῖς κλητοῖς` → *unto them that are called* giving *unto them* to `αὐτοῖς` and *that are called* to `κλητοῖς`. Rule 76's availability test does not reach this: an antecedent is the very word the relative clause is predicated of rather than an English word of some other role, so a pronoun that has written it is spent for this purpose and not available to the article. Rule 90 is the near contrast and is untouched: where the ASV writes only one English word for the pair that word is the article's, being pronoun and relativizer at once, and this clause reaches only a phrase for which the ASV writes more. Rule 22 is the contrast only where no participle follows: `οἱ μετ' αὐτοῦ` → *they … that are with him* keeps the discontinuous *they … that* on the article, since a prepositional phrase has no verb to carry a relativizer, and the copula goes with `μετά`. That is the only configuration in which an article carries *of him who* or *that which* whole. A reference comparison will report such an `unrepresented` article as a disagreement, and that report is not a correction.
amendments.why: 1CO.1 wrote the same apposition twice and analysed it two ways, which is the split this pass corrected. Rule 32's 'supplies the pronoun and nothing else' does not say what happens when the pronoun is already spelled by another token, and the sentence as it stood reads as licensing the article a relativizer instead — which is how 1CO.1.18 was first aligned. Rule 20 already states the principle for a noun complement and names Ὑμῖν ... τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, so this is a narrowing of rule 32's own over-broad sentence rather than a new claim, and it is returned as an amendment so the correction stands where a verse pass will read it. Rule 90's single-word arm is preserved verbatim and explicitly scoped out, so the hard-won relaxation it records is not dropped.

conventions: Where an expressed Greek pronoun stands in apposition to an articular substantive and the ASV recasts the phrase as a finite relative clause, the pronoun's own English is the antecedent, so the article has no pronoun left to supply and is its own unrepresented unit; the complement carries the supplied relativizer, any copula and its own word. τοῖς δὲ σῳζομένοις ἡμῖν -> 'unto us who are saved' gives 'unto us' to ἡμῖν, nothing to the article and 'who are saved' to the participle at 1.18, exactly as αὐτοῖς δὲ τοῖς κλητοῖς -> 'unto them that are called' does at 1.24. The complement's class does not change it: a participle and a verbal adjective are treated alike here. The contrast within the chapter is an articular participle with no pronoun in apposition, where the article takes the pronoun in the ordinary way (1.18 s007, 1.21, 1.31) or the single relativizer under rule 90 (1.2).

Rule 70's counting test, stated there for τε ... καί, is carried in this chapter to a correlative καί ... καί and to a three-member τε ... καί ... καί series, the number of English conjunctions the ASV wrote deciding it. At 1.22 the ASV writes one 'and' for two correlative καί, so the second takes it and the first is unrepresented; at 1.30 it writes three conjunctions for τε, καί and καί, so each particle keeps one; at 1.28 it writes three connectives for three καί, so each keeps one. Count the English conjunctions before asking which particle is which.

report: One genuine cross-verse split. The construction 'dative pronoun + article + substantival complement recast as a finite relative clause' was analysed two ways. 1CO.1.24 (αὐτοῖς δὲ τοῖς κλητοῖς -> unto them that are called) leaves the article unrepresented because αὐτοῖς has already written the antecedent; 1CO.1.18 (τοῖς δὲ σῳζομένοις ἡμῖν -> unto us who are saved) gave the article the relativizer 'who' while ἡμῖν took 'unto us'. Nothing in the source licenses the difference, and the participle at 1.18 argues the other way: rule 32 gives the relativizer to the participle and the article the pronoun and nothing else, and rule 20 names this very case (Ὑμῖν ... τοῖς ἔθνεσιν -> to you that are Gentiles). Patched 1CO.1.18 to 1CO.1.24's reading; 1CO.1.24 stands as written.

Checked and cleared as licensed, not splits: τοὺς σοφούς -> 'them that are wise' against τὰ ἰσχυρά -> 'the things that are strong' within 1.27, the ASV writing an antecedent pronoun in one and a determiner plus supplied nominal in the other; τοῖς -> 'that' at 1.2 against 'to them' at 1.18 s007, 'them' at 1.21 and 'He' at 1.31, which is rule 90's single-word arm against rule 32's ordinary split, decided by the count of English words the ASV wrote; every article before a determinerless God or Christ emptied under rule 23 (1.2, 1.4, 1.6, 1.9, 1.14, 1.17, 1.20, 1.21, 1.25, 1.27, 1.28, 1.29); the three μέν all unrepresented under rule 70; the four μή, each a different construction (rule 59 at 1.7, rule 44 at 1.13, plain negator at 1.10 and 1.28, rule 87 join at 1.29); the support-verb frames all headed on the meaning-bearing complement at 1.17, 1.19, 1.20, 1.21, 1.27 and 1.28.

Supplied-word treatments were read end to end, the candidate table being blind to added units. 'to be' folds onto κλητός at 1.1 and 1.2; 'that ye be' folds onto the standing predicate adjective at 1.8; 'that are of the household' folds onto Χλόης under rule 52 at 1.11; the repeated complementizers fold as rule 103 helpers at 1.10; and the two added units, 'Lord' at 1.2 and 'are called' at 1.26, are both words whose licensing token is already spent. That division is consistent: a supplied word folds where a standing token's English is still incomplete and is added where it is not.

BSB: none of the six disagreements is a genuine error. The three genitive articles at 1.6, 1.17 and 1.29 stand before a determinerless God or Christ (rule 23); μή at 1.7 is rule 59's redundant negative and at 1.13 rule 44's interrogative, which the contract states in terms is not a correction; τοῖς at 1.24 is rule 20's stated contrast. The patch to 1.18 makes τοῖς there a seventh disagreement. That is a consequence of the convention the chapter now holds uniformly, not a score decision, and no accepted edge was changed to move the aggregate.

Recorded two conventions and one amendment, to rule 32 rather than a new rule, so that the over-broad 'supplies the pronoun and nothing else' is corrected where it stands rather than cross-referenced.
